title: Momentum
question: What is momentum?

principle.name: Momentum
principle.formulaNote: momentum = mass × velocity, in kg·m/s. In any collision or explosion with no outside push, the total momentum before equals the total after.
principle.idea: Momentum is how much 'oomph' a moving thing carries: its mass times its velocity. When things collide or push apart, momentum passes from one to the other, but the total never changes.
principle.discovered: 1644–1687 · Descartes's 'quantity of motion', corrected by Huygens and Wallis (1668), made law by Newton

examples.title: Crumple zones and airbags
examples.text: A crash takes away all of a car's momentum. Crumple zones, belts and airbags stretch the stop from milliseconds to about a tenth of a second, cutting the force on the people inside many times.

examples.title: Car meets lorry
examples.text: Locked together after a head-on crash, the wreck moves with the total momentum. A 16 t lorry barely slows; a 1.2 t car's speed changes by more than its own crash speed.

examples.title: Why the helmet has foam
examples.text: A rider's head must lose its momentum whatever happens. A helmet's 3 cm foam liner stretches that stop about five times longer than bare skull, keeping the peak under the 275 g test limit.

examples.title: Riding into a stop
examples.text: A 90 kg bike and rider at 20 km/h carry 500 kg·m/s. Brakes remove it gently over seconds; a kerb does it in a few hundredths of a second, which is why you go over the bars.

examples.title: A fan is a gentle rocket
examples.text: A 1,200 mm ceiling fan throws about 4 kg of air down each second at 3 m/s. That momentum per second, about 13 N, pushes the fan upwards.

examples.title: Rockets in empty space
examples.text: Throwing exhaust back at 3 km/s gives the rocket the same momentum forwards, no air needed. Tsiolkovsky's 1903 equation turns that into the rocket's final speed.

examples.title: Newton's cradle
examples.text: Lift two balls and two come out. One ball at double speed would keep momentum but double the energy, so hard steel balls choose the only answer that keeps both.

examples.title: Giving with the hands
examples.text: A fielder who draws her hands back 40 cm makes a catch last 40 times longer than stiff hands, so the same momentum arrives with a fortieth of the force.

examples.title: Sailing on sunlight
examples.text: Light carries momentum. In 2010 JAXA's IKAROS spread a 14 m sail and measured a push of about 1.1 millinewtons from sunlight alone.

hook: Why does a lorry shove a car backwards in a crash, why does a helmet have foam, and why does a Newton's cradle send out exactly two balls when you drop two? Crash carts, cars and carrom strikers, fire a cannon and a rocket, catch a cricket ball, and sail on sunlight.

explainer.title: Mass on the move
explainer.text: Momentum is mass times velocity, p = m v, in kg·m/s, and it has a direction. Measure m on a scale and v with light gates, and multiply. When two carts collide or spring apart, whatever one loses the other gains, so the total is the same before and after: bouncy, sticky or explosive. Kinetic energy is only kept in the bouncy case.

explainer.title: Crashes and catches
explainer.text: After a head-on crash the wreck moves with the total momentum, so a lorry barely slows while a car's Δv is huge. Stopping anything needs an impulse, F × Δt = Δp. Crumple zones, belts, airbags, helmet foam and soft hands all stretch Δt so the peak force, in g, falls.

explainer.title: Push-offs
explainer.text: Start at zero momentum and push apart: skaters, a boat and its jumper, a cannon and its ball end with equal and opposite momentum. A rocket keeps throwing exhaust back, Δv = v_e ln(full ÷ empty), and a ceiling fan's thrust is the air's momentum per second, about 13 N.

explainer.title: Games
explainer.text: Newton's cradle sends out as many balls as you drop, because only that keeps both momentum and energy; clay balls crawl off together. On a carrom board momentum adds as arrows, and equal pool balls split at 90°. A cricket bat reverses the ball's momentum in about a millisecond.

explainer.title: Myths and limits
explainer.text: In a crash both vehicles feel the same force; the heavier one just changes speed less, and the wreck goes the way of more momentum. Momentum isn't energy: same p, a lighter, faster ball digs a far deeper dent. Spin has its own conserved momentum, L = I ω, and even light pushes: IKAROS, 2010.

concepts.def: Mass times velocity, p = m v, in kg·m/s. It has a size and a direction.
With no outside push, the total momentum of colliding or exploding objects stays the same.
Force × time, F Δt, in N·s. It equals the change of momentum, so a longer stop means a smaller force.
Elastic collisions keep kinetic energy too; inelastic ones turn some of it into heat, sound and dents.
The change of velocity in a collision, the best single measure of how much a crash hurts.
The push from throwing mass away: mass per second × speed. Rockets and fans both work this way.
The momentum of spinning, L = I ω, also conserved. Light carries momentum too: p = E ÷ c.
